Assuming the standard student-proposing deferred acceptance (DA) mechanism is used, truthful reporting is a dominant strategy for students. DA ensures you cannot get a strictly better outcome by misrepresenting preferences given the schools' priorities.

Given your true preferences (y > x > z > w) and priorities (priority 1 at y and w; priority 2 at x and z), you already have top priority at your top choice y, so listing y first maximizes your chance of getting it. Although many applicants also prefer y > x > w > z, your priority 1 at y protects you against that competition. Elevating a lower-preferred but safe school (e.g., listing w higher to exploit your priority 1 there) could only hurt your chance of getting a more-preferred school under DA. Therefore report your true ranking.
reasoning.Student B:
Assuming the standard student-proposing deferred acceptance (DA) mechanism (the usual school-choice setting where students apply in order of their submitted ranking and schools use fixed priorities), truthful ranking is a dominant strategy. That means I should list my true preferences y > x > w > z. 

Even though many applicants favor y and my priority at y (2) is lower than at x (1), ranking x above y to try to “play safe” cannot improve my outcome under DA: by ranking y first I get considered for y and only go to x if rejected from y, which is weakly better than applying to x first. (If the mechanism were not DA—e.g., Boston—different strategic considerations could apply, but no other mechanism was specified.)

reasoning.Student D:
My true preference is x > y > w > z. I consider two strategic points:

1) Mechanism: If the system uses student-proposing deferred acceptance (DA), truthful reporting is a dominant strategy, so I should rank schools in my true order.

2) Competition & priorities: Most applicants favor y first, so y will be highly competitive. My priorities are relatively low at x and w (4) and a bit better at y and z (3). Even though I have slightly better priority at y, the heavy demand for y makes it unlikely I would win a seat there. Listing x first gives me the best chance of being matched to my top-choice (and is consistent with truthful play). Misreporting to try to game a different mechanism (e.g., ranking a less-preferred but less-contested school first) doesn’t improve my outcome given my low priorities at x/w and high demand for y.

Therefore I submit my true ranking: x > y > w > z.
